title: History Maker award, thinking without thinking, and Baldwin on The Making of Jazz
summary: Jang cites a YouTube tribute, Bruce Lee and Gladwell's Blink, embracing paradox, and James Baldwin's response to James Lincoln Collier.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: talk about, but it doesn’t — I’m not sure it really expresses who I am. So and we can’t go into the whole — I mean I already spent too much time on my childhood, about the railroad. But yet, actually, let me put it another way. If you’re interested, on YouTube I recently was awarded the History Maker award by the Chinese Historical Society of America, last month. That was September 21st. And they did a three minute YouTube, or a three or four minute YouTube. And I open up where I saw well I’m just like my father, who I didn’t know, he died when I was two years old. And I said during the 1930’s, my father, who was five-foot two, would dance with a six-foot two blonde, you know, which was taboo. And then, so he would — I think I made a statement that says most Chinese Americans I know, of my generation, are afraid to take chances. So for me, it’s like you do it. It’s like Bruce Lee, you don’t have time to think. Actually Bruce Lee said thinking without thinking. Which I’m wondering, Malcolm Gladwell wrote the book Blink. I don’t know if you’re familiar with that. That’s the second book after Tipping Point. It’s called thinking without thinking. But he does not identify with Bruce Lee at all in that book. But that’s who I am is the thinking without thinking. Oh and also, okay, as artists, we embrace paradox. So oh, that’s what it is about this country. You know it’s black and white. People want the black and white answers. Just like the national anthem. Artists, we embrace paradox. And I’ll say one more thing is that James Baldwin wrote a powerful response to James Lincoln Collier’s The Making of Jazz which was published in 1979, James Lincoln Collier the prominent writer who graduated from Hamilton College in 1952. And James Lincoln Collier wrote this article in 1979, it was called “The Cross of Redemption, of Sorrow Songs.” And it got republished recently. That’s the title of the book. It’s only seven pages long. But he will say you can’t study history from a distance. Then he comes back and contradicts himself and says you can study history from a safe distance. So that’s a perfect — it’s a powerful article. And when we’re finished recording I’d like to get your perspective and reflections about The Making of Jazz both from the book and your interview with James Lincoln Collier.
